project-management-u3-1-project-manageme: Scope: one digital menu board screen showing prices, daily specials and allergy symbols. Time: two weeks to design, check with the manager and install. Resources: the student, Canva, a school laptop and the TV screen. Client brief: the manager's requirements, such as allergy symbols that are clear enough to read from the counter.

Adding a 10-second animated special each day increases the scope. With the same two-week deadline, the project needs more resources, such as animation software or a second student, or the manager must accept a simpler animation or a later date. If none of these change, the quality of the other parts of the menu board could suffer.
project-management-u3-2-design-process-c: 1. Age: the audience is adults over 50, so text should be large and the voiceover clear and not too fast, so it is easy to read and hear on a gym screen. 2. Experience: many may be new to boxing, so the video should show beginners training safely, not fit athletes, so viewers feel the class is for them.
1. The class day and time are on screen for at least 5 seconds. 2. All text is readable from 3 metres away. 3. The video is no longer than 20 seconds.
project-management-u3-3-representing-the: The student could draw several small, quick thumbnail sketches of different layouts for the home page, such as a banner above or beside the repair menu. She can compare them and choose the best one before spending time on detailed design.

1. The menu runs across the top of every page, so customers can reach Bookings from any page. 2. A large 'Book a repair' button in a contrasting colour sits above the fold, so the main action is easy to find.
project-management-u3-4-evaluating-digit: 1. Survey: ask 10 students to rate whether the video made them want to attend, which shows whether the video achieved its purpose. 2. Check against the criteria: play the video with a stopwatch to see whether the date and venue are on screen for at least 5 seconds, which gives measurable evidence.
1. The video is no longer than 30 seconds. 2. The school logo appears in the final frame.
managing-data-1-file-optimisation-q1: An 18 MB photo is a large file, so it takes a long time to download, especially on mobile data. The home page therefore loads slowly, and visitors may leave before it appears.
managing-data-1-file-optimisation-q2: For the website, the photo should be reduced to a small size, such as about 1200 pixels wide, saved in RGB colour as a compressed JPEG so it loads quickly on screen. For the yearbook, it needs a higher resolution, about 300 PPI at the printed size, usually in CMYK, so the print is sharp. The file will be larger, but print quality matters more than download speed.
managing-data-2-compression-q1: Compression reduces file size, so files transfer faster and use less storage.
managing-data-2-compression-q2: For the label, use lossless compression, such as WAV or FLAC, because mastering needs every detail of the original recording. For fans, use lossy compression, such as MP3, because the small files download quickly and the loss of quality is hardly noticeable.
managing-data-3-cropping-and-resampling-: She could crop out the unneeded areas around the building, such as sky and ground. Fewer pixels are stored and the building becomes the focus of the image.

The photo is much larger than the 600-pixel box it fills. Resampling (downsampling) the photo to about 600 pixels wide removes pixels the box cannot display, so each image is much smaller and the PDF shrinks from 80 MB.
managing-data-4-online-data-management-q: 1. Use a consistent naming convention, such as Name_Task_v01, so the group can find each file and see which version is current. 2. Organise the folder into subfolders for each section of the project, so files are easy to find and not mixed up.
The group could give each student edit rights only to their own files, with the others set to view or comment only. Then a student could not delete someone else's work by mistake.
managing-data-5-version-control-q1: Document version control is managing changes to a file so the current version is clear and earlier versions can be retrieved if needed.
managing-data-5-version-control-q2: 1. Keep one master file in OneDrive and use its version history, so there is only one current copy and she can restore earlier drafts. 2. Name files with version numbers and dates, such as Essay_v03_2026-03-14, so she can see which version contains her teacher's feedback.
managing-data-6-cloud-computing-q1: Cloud computing means data and software are stored and run on remote servers, owned by a provider, and users access them over the internet instead of using their own equipment.
managing-data-6-cloud-computing-q2: Advantage: staff can access client files and accounting software from home or at client offices, so they can work anywhere. Disadvantage: client financial data is held by a third party, which is a privacy risk, and staff cannot work if the internet goes down.
managing-data-7-maintenance-utilities-q1: 1. Disk clean-up: removes temporary files, which frees space on her nearly full SSD. 2. Clearing the browser cache and history: deletes stored data built up over two years, which saves space and helps the browser run faster.
managing-data-7-maintenance-utilities-q2: An SSD has no moving parts and reaches every storage location equally quickly, so fragmented files do not slow it down. Defragmenting would not help and adds unnecessary wear.
managing-data-8-security-utilities-q1: Spyware. It secretly installs on a computer, collects information such as passwords, and sends it to someone else, which explains how the parent's bank password was used.
managing-data-8-security-utilities-q2: 1. Run an updated anti-malware scan to find and remove the spyware. 2. Change the bank password on a safe device and turn on two-factor authentication, so a stolen password alone cannot be used to log in.
networks-1-networking-concepts-q1: A network connects the four computers so they can share files, printers and one internet connection. Staff no longer need USB drives, and the office needs fewer printers and internet connections.
networks-1-networking-concepts-q2: Advantage: staff can share files straight away instead of using USB drives, which saves time. Disadvantage: if the network fails, all computers lose access to shared files and the printer, and the office is also more exposed to viruses spreading between computers.
networks-2-transmission-media-q1: Optic fibre. The shed is 400 m from the house, which is beyond the 100 m limit of Ethernet cable. Optic fibre carries data at high speed over long distances and is not affected by electrical interference from farm machinery.
networks-2-transmission-media-q2: Wired media, such as Ethernet cable, give a fast and reliable connection with little interference, but devices must stay plugged in and cables run through the house. Wireless media, such as Wi-Fi, let phones and laptops move around the house without cables, but the signal can be slower and weaker through walls.
networks-3-transmission-rates-q1: Transmission rate is the amount of data sent per second, measured in bits per second, such as Mbps.
networks-3-transmission-rates-q2: The connection's bandwidth is shared with the family streaming TV, so less is available for his stream. His upload rate is only 20 Mbps, much lower than download, and live streaming needs upload. A solution is to use a wired connection, lower the stream quality, or move to a plan with a higher upload rate.
networks-4-network-components-q1: The router directs data between the studio's LAN and the internet, and between devices. The modem converts the signal from the internet provider so the studio's network can connect to the internet.
networks-4-network-components-q2: The NIC (network interface card) is the hardware that physically connects a computer to the network, wired or wireless. Without it, the computer cannot send or receive data on the network.
networks-5-lan-topologies-q1: In a wired star topology every device is connected by its own cable to a central switch. Data passes through the switch, so if one cable fails, the other devices keep working.
networks-5-lan-topologies-q2: The clinic should use client-server. 1. Patient records are stored centrally on the server, where security can be controlled. 2. The server can be backed up daily in one place. 3. Access to records can be controlled by user accounts, so only authorised staff see patient data. Peer-to-peer would leave records spread across staff computers.
networks-6-designing-a-home-lan-q1: Router: at the NBN point in the garage, because the internet connection arrives there and it needs to connect to it directly. Wireless access point: upstairs, in a central position, so the home office and bedrooms get a strong signal through the floor.
networks-6-designing-a-home-lan-q2: A wired connection is reliable for work video calls, so calls do not drop out. It is faster for uploading large files than Wi-Fi, and it does not lose signal through the floor to the upstairs office.
impacts-of-technology-u4-1-privacy-act-c: No. The school name is not needed to sell a concert ticket. Under the Privacy Act, an organisation should only collect personal information that is necessary for its function.
A customer has the right to ask to see the personal information an organisation holds about them, and to ask for incorrect or out-of-date details to be corrected.
impacts-of-technology-u4-2-identity-thef: Criminals could use the names, addresses, dates of birth and licence numbers to pretend to be a customer, for example to open a credit card or take out a loan in that person's name.

1. Keep the data secure, using protections such as strong passwords, encryption and access controls, so hackers cannot steal it. 2. Notify affected customers and the regulator when a serious data breach happens, so customers can protect themselves. (Destroying data no longer needed is another responsibility.)
impacts-of-technology-u4-3-digital-divid: The digital divide is the gap between people who have access to, and the skills to use, digital technologies and those who do not.

Older residents who lack app skills or a smartphone can no longer bank locally, so they must travel to another town. People with poor internet in the country area may not be able to use the app reliably, so they cannot access their money or pay bills.
impacts-of-technology-u4-4-electronic-co: Electronic commerce is buying and selling goods or services over the internet.

Positive: customers can order birthday cakes at any time, including at night, so the bakery can take more orders and sell more. Negative: orders can arrive outside opening hours, so a small family business may have to check and respond to orders at all hours, which adds to workload.
impacts-of-technology-u4-5-dependency-on: If staff cannot use the app and video calls, they cannot do their jobs, and if patients cannot use them, they cannot book appointments or see results. Training and support are therefore needed so everyone can use the system.
Patients should use a strong password and not share their login details, so no one else can see their health information.
application-skills-u4-1-online-collabora: 1. Shared cloud storage, such as OneDrive: all three can store and access the video files, script and music in one place, even though they live in different towns. 2. Video conferencing, such as Teams: the group can talk, share screens and plan the video together without meeting in person.
Slow internet in one town may make uploading and downloading large video files difficult, so the group may be delayed, and time zones or availability may make it harder to meet.
application-skills-u4-2-web-authoring-fe: 1. Internal link: connects pages within the club site, such as from Home to Fixtures, so visitors can move around. 2. Email link: opens a new message to the club secretary, so visitors can contact the club quickly. (An external link to the league website would also earn marks.)
A .css file controls colours and fonts for every page that links to it. The student would change the brand colour in one place, instead of editing each of the five pages.
application-skills-u4-3-navigation-maps-: Hierarchical. The pages are arranged in levels, with the Cover at the top and sections such as Animals and Map below. It suits the zoo guide because visitors choose a section from the cover and return to it easily.
1. All five pages shown as boxes and labelled. 2. Arrows between pages showing the direction of each link.
application-skills-u4-4-responsive-desig: Responsive design means a website's layout adjusts automatically to the size of the screen or device, so it is easy to use on a phone, tablet or computer.

1. Change the wide menu table into a single column at phone width, so customers do not need to scroll sideways. 2. Make the buttons larger and spaced apart at phone width, so they are easy to tap without zooming in.
application-skills-u4-5-animation-softwa: Set a start keyframe with the logo off-screen to the left and fully transparent, and an end keyframe with the logo in its final position and fully visible. The software creates the frames in between (a tween), so the logo slides in and fades in smoothly.
A button lets the user interact with the animation and triggers an action when it is clicked. Its states are up (normal), over (when the mouse is on it) and down (when it is clicked).
project-management-u4-1-plan-of-action-q: Each row should include the task, the time allocated, the resources needed, the person responsible and the due date. (Whether the task is complete is also acceptable.)

1. Draft the program layout: 3 hours, laptop and Canva. 2. Get approval from the drama teacher: 15 minutes, printed draft. 3. Make changes and print the final copies: 2 hours, laptop and school printer.
project-management-u4-2-time-management-: 1. Break the documentary into tasks with deadlines, such as filming interviews by week 1, so they can see what must be finished each week. 2. Use a Gantt chart or timeline, so they can see that editing must start by week 3 and keep on track.
Buffer time is extra time in the plan. Unexpected problems, such as a missed interview or museum feedback needing changes, can be fixed without missing the four-week deadline.
project-management-u4-3-resources-q1: Hardware: a camera or phone and a laptop. Software: InDesign. People: the park ranger, who gives feedback, and test users.
project-management-u4-3-resources-q2: Photos: back them up to OneDrive after each trail visit and name them by trail, so none are lost or confused. Park ranger: book a feedback time in the plan in advance and send the draft early, so the ranger has time to respond before the deadline.
project-management-u4-4-evaluation-q1: 1. Survey or questionnaire: ask restaurant staff and customers whether the menu was clear and attractive, which gives opinions from the people who use it. 2. Checklist of criteria: tick off the design criteria, such as 'all prices are readable', which gives clear evidence of what was and was not met.
project-management-u4-4-evaluation-q2: Book the photo session in week 1 with a backup date. The photos took twice as long as planned, so booking earlier with a backup would have kept the project on schedule.
